title: Ripples become an ocean
hook: one glimpse swallows Ajamila's life; the sutras on ripples and who crosses
carry: dussanga turns ripples into an ocean
tomorrow: A taste that can't be told

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the company of great souls: hard to find, hard to fathom, never failing, and no difference between the Lord and his people.

In the Bhagavata Purana, Ajamila is a young Brahmin with a good name: learned, gentle, careful in his duties. One day his father sends him to the forest for flowers and kindling. On the way home he sees a man and a woman of the town, drunk and laughing in each other's arms. It's one glimpse. He tries to steady his mind with all he's studied, and can't. He keeps thinking of her, keeps going back, and the thought is fed until it swallows everything: his father's wealth, his young wife, his good name. Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras give that a picture: ripples becoming an ocean.
screen: `ONE GLIMPSE ON THE ROAD.` → `FED, DAY AFTER DAY.` → `IT SWALLOWS A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bad company, dussanga, is to be given up in every way, the sutras say. And they give the reason as a chain. It causes desire, then anger, then delusion, then the loss of memory, then the loss of understanding, and then the loss of everything. Then the image: though these arise only like ripples, through company they become an ocean. A flash of desire or anger isn't a disaster in itself. A ripple is a ripple. What turns it into an ocean is company: whatever keeps feeding it, a person, a place, a feed on a screen. Many teachers read Ajamila's fall exactly this way: one glimpse, fed day after day. Then a question, asked twice: who crosses? Who crosses over maya, the great illusion? The answers come in short lines. The one who gives up clinging, serves the great, becomes free of mine, goes beyond the pairs of opposites, like pleasure and pain, and comes to a love that doesn't break off. That one crosses, that one crosses, and helps the worlds cross too. And Ajamila? You met his ending in earlier years: old and afraid of death, he called his son's name, Narayana, and Vishnu's messengers came. The Bhagavata says he then went to Haridwar on the Ganga and gave his last years to devotion. Even the man the ocean swallowed got across. That's why Hindu families guard their company and seek out satsang: in this teaching, the mind takes the shape of what it keeps near.
screen: `DUSSANGA: A CHAIN OF LOSSES.` · `RIPPLES BECOME AN OCEAN.` · `WHO CROSSES? WHO CROSSES?` · `EVEN AJAMILA CROSSED.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later something will rise, an irritation, a wanting, a worry; notice it the way you'd notice a ripple on water. Don't push it down and don't feed it, no replaying the argument, no adding the next thought; just watch it rise and flatten out on its own. If you pray, you can hand each ripple to God as it passes.
Bhakti. In the sutras, it's guarded from the company that turns ripples into an ocean, and it carries those who cross.
Your line: dussanga turns ripples into an ocean. A ripple left unfed stays a ripple. Rest well.

dussanga.meaning: bad company, to be given up in every way

maya.meaning: the great illusion, which the devotee crosses

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna

Narada Bhakti Sutras.meaning: a short book on love of God, attributed to Narada

Ajamila.meaning: a Brahmin who fell through one fed desire, and was saved by the Name

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 43–50 (bad company; the chain of losses; ripples become an ocean; who crosses maya; he crosses and helps the worlds cross)

notes: Sutras 43–50 paraphrased. Sutra 49 (giving up even the Vedas and gaining unbroken love) is summarized only as 'comes to a love that doesn't break off'; the line about the Vedas is left out to avoid a misreading without its commentary. Confirm this is acceptable.

Sutra 47's 'goes beyond the three gunas' is also left out for length; 'seeks out a quiet place' renders vivikta-sthānaṃ sevate; 'loosens the knots that tie them to the world' renders loka-bandham unmūlayati (literally uproots); 'worrying over getting and keeping' renders yoga-kṣemaṃ tyajati. Confirm.
The comparison with Gita 2.62–63 is stated as 'much like it'; the Gita's chain begins with dwelling on objects and attachment. Confirm.
'A feed on a screen' and the closing boat image are the script's own illustrations.
Editor pass: 'link by link' cut from the Gita comparison, since the Gita's chain begins differently (dwelling on objects, attachment).
